newsitem.title: PERU: Savage among seekers for Peru mine.
newsitem.headline: Savage among seekers for Peru mine.

text.p: Peru's Minera Volcan may have a modest history but the medium-sized zinc miner is ambitious and wants to elbow aside some of the world's top miners at the government's next asset sale, analysts said.
The precocious bid is possible thanks to a deal last year with the government that has completely rejuvenated the firm, they said.

Since exchanging its concessions worked under contract for outright ownership of other deposits, Volcan has cast off the burden of hefty royalty payments and has such strong growth prospects it believes it can compete with the best.

"The fact that Volcan is now owner of its concessions both gives it greater muscle in the market of the medium-sized miners and enables it to grow," said Manuel Torres, mining analyst at consulting firm Finvest.
Encouraged by elevated zinc prices on international markets, Volcan also hopes to beat its annual 10 percent growth of 1996 in the next two years, a company official, who asked not to be named, said.

The arena for Volcan's 'David-and-Goliath' style bid will be the government's July auction of the Mahr Tunel mining asset, whose $50 million minimum bid price tag and obligation for the buyer to invest a further $60 million has squeezed out other second-tier firms.
Volcan appears small fry even to Peru's top miners Minsur and Morococha, who are also lining up to buy the asset, but alongside the foreign giants entering the auction the local miner is dwarfed.
Mexico's Industrias Penoles -- the world's largest refined silver producer -- will be just one of the heavyweights Volcan takes on.

Last month, Penoles bought the biggest asset in the government's sweeping program of privatizations -- the huge La Oroya metallurgic complex -- and is determined to snare the nearby Mahr Tunel mines to feed its score of smelters and refineries.
Following Penoles are Switzerland's Glencore -- already the owner of the country's largest zinc mine -- Australia's Savage, Mexico's Grupo Mexico, the United State's Sunshine and Sweden's Boliden.
But Volcan's enthusiasm for the auction is not just a case of blind ambition, according to the analysts.

"It is logical Volcan should be interested in the privatization of Mahr Tunel, because its operations are right next door and it knows the geology inside out," said Julio Alcalde, mining analyst at consultants MGS y Asociados.

Volcan's main production unit at Carahuacra, 200 miles (310 km) notheast of Lima in the department of Junin, lies close to Mahr Tunel, which controls the San Cristobal and Andaychagua mines. Last year, San Cristobal produced 680,000 dry tonnes of ore containing zinc, lead, copper and silver, while Andaychagua produced about 395,000 dry tonnes of ore with silver, lead and zinc.

At the end of 1996, Volcan paid state miner Centromin $4.2 million for Carahuacra and its two million tonnes of proven and probable mineral reserves with a high zinc content of 8.5 percent per tonne as well as some lead and silver.

It is also fair to assume that Volcan, which recorded a net profit last year of around $3 million dollars and sales revenue of over $20 million, was capable of competing with its richer rivals at the Mahr Tunel auction, Alcalde said.
But if the miner should fail in its bid to buy the asset, "it will surely start to receive buy-out offers from the winner", he added.

That possibility has catapulted the miner's shares on the Lima Sock Exchange from its usual position as a lower tier stock to one of the more heavily traded companies. Volcan's liquid labor share has soared almost 700 percent this year to above 13.40 soles per share.

The miner is an attractive play on the bolsa due to its liquid stock, which is owned jointly by a a group of minority shareholders headed by holding company Hazel Investments, which owns a 24 percent stake.
